case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, under AEDPA, the Fourth Circuit correctly held that Maryland unreasonably applied clearly established Supreme Court Brady materiality precedent by treating the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence as immaterial based largely on the remaining evidence’s apparent strength (i.e., using a sufficiency-like approach rather than the cumulative Kyles materiality analysis).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1) (AEDPA—"contrary to" / "unreasonable application" of clearly established federal law) as applied to the Due Process Brady obligation under the Fourteenth Amendment (Brady v. Maryland materiality standard).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The State (Klein, Superintendent, et al.) argues that the suppressed evidence was not material under Brady because, even if disclosed, the remaining trial evidence was sufficient to sustain the verdict; the state appellate court identified the correct governing rule (Kyles/Strickler) and reasonably applied it, so AEDPA deference bars federal habeas relief.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Martin argues that clearly established Supreme Court law (especially Kyles) forbids a sufficiency-of-the-evidence style materiality analysis; courts must cumulatively assess how the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence would have altered the whole evidentiary picture—adding force to the defense case and subtracting force from the prosecution case—particularly where impeachment would significantly weaken a key witness and the prosecution relied on that witness in instructions/closing; Maryland’s court unreasonably applied Kyles, so § 2254(d)(1) is satisfied.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan press the strongest point for Respondent: Kyles makes clear Brady materiality is not a sufficiency-of-the-evidence test, and Maryland’s emphasis on other inculpatory proof—especially after assuming the suppressed report could seriously impeach a key witness—creates the appearance of a forbidden shortcut. But under § 2254(d)(1) the question is not whether Maryland’s reasoning was imperfect or even whether we would characterize the analysis differently; it is whether the adjudication was an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established law. As Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Maryland cited the correct Kyles/Strickler reasonable-probability standard, and its discussion of the remaining evidence can fairly be read as part of the cumulative “confidence in the verdict” inquiry rather than a categorical sufficiency rule. Given Richter’s requirement that relief be reserved for decisions beyond any possibility for fairminded disagreement, Respondent has not cleared AEDPA’s threshold on the state-court record.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan press the best argument for Respondent: that Maryland’s discussion of the remaining evidence looks like the sufficiency-style shortcut Kyles said has “no place” in Brady materiality, especially after assuming the suppressed report could “totally discredit” a key witness. But AEDPA requires more than identifying language that could be read as imperfect; under Richter we must deny relief unless the state court’s materiality determination is beyond any possibility for fairminded disagreement. As the Chief Justice and Justice Alito explain, Maryland recited the correct Kyles/Strickler “reasonable probability/undermines confidence” standard, and its reference to other inculpatory proof can reasonably be understood as part of the cumulative confidence-in-the-verdict inquiry rather than adoption of a categorical sufficiency test. Given that permissible reading, Respondent has not shown an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established holdings under § 2254(d)(1).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan rightly underscore Kyles’s admonition that Brady materiality is not a sufficiency test, and Maryland’s phrasing—especially assuming the report could "totally discredit" a witness—invites that critique. But under § 2254(d)(1) the dispositive question is whether the state court’s adjudication was an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established Kyles/Strickler, and as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, Maryland expressly identified the "reasonable probability"/"undermines confidence" standard and then discussed the suppressed impeachment in light of the trial record. That discussion can reasonably be read as the permissible, totality-of-the-evidence assessment Kyles requires, not a categorical rule that "enough remains" ends the inquiry; Richter instructs us to deny relief where fairminded jurists could so read the opinion. Given that plausible reading, I cannot say the Fourth Circuit’s contrary construction satisfies AEDPA’s demanding threshold.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s point that AEDPA deference is an antecedent hurdle, and that a state court’s citation to Kyles/Strickler plus discussion of remaining evidence can, in some cases, reflect the permissible cumulative “confidence in the verdict” inquiry. But Maryland’s own reasoning—assuming the suppressed forensic information could “totally discredit” a featured witness and then pivoting to the existence of other inculpatory evidence as essentially dispositive—tracks the sufficiency-style shortcut Kyles says has “no place” in Brady materiality. As Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson note, reciting the right words cannot insulate an analysis that functionally collapses materiality into “the case was still strong,” rather than asking how disclosure would reshape the evidentiary picture for a reasonable decisionmaker. On this record, the Fourth Circuit did not simply reweigh; it identified a structural misapplication of clearly established Brady law, which is an unreasonable application under § 2254(d)(1).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s central point—that AEDPA is an independent threshold and Richter requires us to credit reasonable readings of a state-court opinion—is right as far as it goes, but it does not answer what Maryland actually did. Even granting the court recited Kyles/Strickler, its analysis assumed the suppressed report could “totally discredit” a featured witness and then pivoted to the existence of other inculpatory evidence as essentially dispositive; that is the sufficiency-style shortcut Kyles says has “no place” in Brady materiality. Richter deference does not permit us to re-characterize a decision whose own reasoning shows the wrong legal lens doing the work; fairminded jurists cannot defend an application that collapses the reasonable-probability/undermined-confidence inquiry into “still enough to convict.” As Justice Sotomayor emphasizes, the problem here is structural misapplication, not merely imperfect phrasing or a debatable weighing of the record.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan press the best argument for Respondent: Kyles warns that Brady materiality is “not a sufficiency of the evidence test,” and Maryland’s pivot to other inculpatory proof—after assuming potent impeachment—can look like the forbidden shortcut. But AEDPA asks an antecedent and independent question, and as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Maryland expressly invoked Kyles/Strickler’s “reasonable probability/undermines confidence” formulation; under Richter, we must deny relief if fairminded jurists could read the opinion as using the remaining-evidence discussion to explain why confidence in the verdict was not undermined rather than to apply a categorical sufficiency rule. Reciting the right standard is not always enough, but here the state court’s reasoning is at least susceptible to a permissible, cumulative verdict-confidence understanding, and § 2254(d)(1) does not allow us to treat debatable analysis as objectively unreasonable. Whatever one might conclude de novo, Respondent has not shown the state adjudication was beyond fairminded disagreement under clearly established holdings as of the time.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan press the hardest point: Kyles says a “strong enough to convict anyway” sufficiency analysis has “no place” in Brady materiality, and Maryland’s opinion—after assuming the report could “totally discredit” a key witness—can be read to pivot to the remaining evidence in a way that resembles that forbidden shortcut. But under AEDPA, as the Chief Justice emphasizes, our threshold task is not to decide whether Maryland’s materiality discussion was ideal; it is whether the adjudication was an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established Kyles/Strickler beyond fairminded disagreement under Richter. Because Maryland expressly recited the correct “reasonable probability/undermines confidence” standard, and because its discussion of other evidence can reasonably be read as part of the cumulative confidence-in-the-verdict inquiry rather than a categorical sufficiency rule, § 2254(d)(1) bars relief even if a de novo court might explain the analysis differently.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan have the strongest point: Maryland’s opinion, especially after assuming the suppressed material could "totally discredit" a key witness, risks sounding like the sufficiency-style shortcut Kyles condemns. But under AEDPA, I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that our task is not to police optimal reasoning; it is to decide whether the state court’s adjudication was an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established Brady law. Because Maryland recited the Kyles/Strickler “reasonable probability/undermines confidence” standard and its discussion of the remaining evidence can reasonably be read—per Richter—as a cumulative verdict-confidence assessment rather than a categorical “enough-to-convict” rule, fairminded jurists could disagree about whether it used the wrong lens. Given that permissible reading, § 2254(d)(1)’s demanding threshold is not met even if the opinion is inartfully framed.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take seriously the Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s point that AEDPA—especially under Richter—requires us to deny relief if the state decision admits of a fairminded reading consistent with Kyles/Strickler, and that a court may reference remaining evidence as part of the “confidence in the verdict” inquiry. But here Maryland’s own analytical move—assuming the suppressed forensics could “totally discredit” a central witness and then pivoting to the existence of other inculpatory proof as effectively dispositive—tracks the sufficiency-style shortcut Kyles expressly rejects, rather than the cumulative, evidence-reframing materiality assessment Brady demands. Reciting the right standard cannot do the operative work when the reasoning reveals a different test driving the outcome, and § 2254(d)(1) does not compel us to treat that as a merely “imperfect” application. On this record, I agree with Justices Sotomayor and Kagan that the Fourth Circuit identified an unreasonable application of clearly established Brady materiality, not a de novo reweighing barred by AEDPA.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under § 2254(d)(1), the question is not whether the Maryland court’s Brady ruling was wrong, but whether it was an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court materiality law on the state-court record. Here the state appellate court expressly identified the governing Kyles/Strickler “reasonable probability” standard and, viewed through AEDPA’s highly deferential lens, its repeated reliance on the strength of the remaining inculpatory evidence can still be understood as a permissible way of explaining why the suppressed laptop/impeachment material did not undermine confidence in the verdict in this case. Kyles clearly rejects a bare sufficiency-of-the-evidence test, but it does not compel habeas relief whenever a state court emphasizes remaining evidence so long as it ultimately applies the reasonable-probability inquiry; the Fourth Circuit, in concluding otherwise, substituted de novo disagreement for the “unreasonable application” determination AEDPA demands. Comity and finality concerns reinforce that, absent a clear Kyles-level misapprehension of the materiality framework, federal habeas relief is barred.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under AEDPA, the question is not whether the state court was wrong about Brady materiality, but whether its merits adjudication was so unjustified that it is beyond any possibility for fairminded disagreement. The “clearly established” rule must be drawn narrowly from this Court’s holdings, and while Kyles states that materiality “is not a sufficiency of evidence test,” it does not clearly establish that any discussion of the remaining evidence’s strength, after reciting the correct reasonable-probability standard, is per se an unreasonable application rather than a permissible way to assess whether the suppressed impeachment would have changed the overall picture. Here, Maryland identified the governing Kyles/Strickler framework and concluded the computer-report impeachment would not, in light of the other trial evidence, create a reasonable probability of a different result; at minimum, fairminded jurists could disagree on that application to these facts. The Fourth Circuit therefore exceeded AEDPA’s limited role by treating the state court’s materiality analysis as categorically improper rather than asking whether the result was indefensible under settled law at the time.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under AEDPA, the question is not whether the Fourth Circuit (or I) would find Brady materiality in the first instance, but whether the Maryland court’s application of clearly established law was so lacking in justification that no fairminded jurist could agree. The state court expressly identified the correct Kyles/Strickler reasonable-probability standard, and it was entitled to consider the totality of the trial evidence—including the remaining inculpatory proof—when deciding whether the suppressed computer report’s impeachment/exculpatory value would have altered the overall evidentiary picture. Kyles bars treating materiality as a pure sufficiency test, but it does not forbid a court from concluding, after weighing the suppressed evidence against countervailing evidence, that confidence in the verdict is not undermined; the Fourth Circuit effectively substituted its own cumulative weighing for the state court’s and thereby failed to give the deference Richter and Williams require. Given the record’s other evidence implicating Martin and the state court’s acknowledgment (but rejection) of the report’s significance, the state-court decision was at least within the range of reasonable applications of Brady.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under § 2254(d)(1), the question is not whether Maryland recited Brady/Kyles, but whether it actually applied Kyles’ cumulative “reasonable probability” framework or instead replaced it with a sufficiency/“strong evidence” shortcut. Here, the state court assumed the suppressed computer-forensics report could have been used to “totally discredit” the prosecution’s key witness linking Martin to the silencer, yet deemed the evidence immaterial largely because other proof remained—precisely the kind of “there would still have been adequate evidence to convict” reasoning Kyles rejects as having “no place” in materiality analysis. That deviation is not a mere disagreement over weighing; it is an unreasonable application of clearly established law because it fails to ask how the suppressed impeachment would alter the overall evidentiary picture for a reasonable decisionmaker, especially where the prosecution’s narrative relied on that witness in argument and the defense theory would be affirmatively strengthened. The Fourth Circuit therefore properly concluded that AEDPA deference did not bar relief.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: AEDPA asks a distinct question from de novo Brady review: not whether I would find materiality myself, but whether Maryland’s materiality determination was so off the mark that no fairminded jurist could accept it. Kyles clearly establishes that materiality is not a sufficiency-of-the-evidence inquiry and requires a cumulative assessment of how suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence would alter the whole evidentiary picture; a state court that largely deems the evidence immaterial because the remaining case looked “strong enough” applies the wrong analytical lens. Given the importance of impeachment when the prosecution featured that witness in closing and instructions, the Fourth Circuit could reasonably conclude that Maryland’s approach unreasonably applied Kyles’s cumulative materiality framework under § 2254(d)(1). Because the state court’s reasoning effectively collapsed Brady materiality into a strength-of-the-rest-of-the-evidence test, AEDPA deference does not bar relief here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: AEDPA § 2254(d)(1) supplies an independent, threshold bar: the question is not whether the Fourth Circuit thought the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence was material under its best reading of Brady, but whether the Maryland court’s materiality determination was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, this Court’s holdings as of the time of the state decision. Kyles clearly establishes that Brady materiality is “not a sufficiency of the evidence test” and requires a cumulative assessment, but a state court does not unreasonably apply Kyles merely by discussing the strength of the remaining evidence so long as it ultimately asks whether disclosure creates a “reasonable probability” of a different result. Because the Maryland court cited the correct governing framework (Brady/Kyles/Strickler) and could reasonably conclude—given the record as a whole—that the undisclosed material would not have altered the verdict’s reliability, fairminded jurists could disagree and AEDPA therefore forecloses habeas relief.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: This case arises on federal habeas, so the threshold question is AEDPA deference under § 2254(d)(1): whether the Maryland court’s decision was not just wrong but an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established Brady/Kyles materiality precedent. Even accepting that Kyles says materiality is “not a sufficiency of the evidence test,” a state court may still consider the strength of the remaining evidence as part of the cumulative “reasonable probability” inquiry, and AEDPA requires giving the state court the benefit of the doubt so long as it identified the correct rule and did not apply a rule that is the opposite of Kyles. On this record, the Fourth Circuit treated the Maryland court’s discussion of the remaining evidence as a forbidden categorical sufficiency test, but the more ordinary reading is that the state court weighed the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory report against the trial record and found no reasonable probability of a different result—at least a reasonable application under Richter/Lockyer’s demanding standard. Because the respondent has not cleared AEDPA’s high bar of showing an unreasonable application (as opposed to mere disagreement with the state court’s materiality assessment), habeas relief should be denied.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: AEDPA requires deference unless the state court’s decision is not just wrong but objectively unreasonable under clearly established law, and Richter instructs that fairminded jurists must be able to disagree. Here the Maryland court recited the correct Brady/Kyles standard and, on this record, its materiality discussion can reasonably be read as assessing whether the suppressed computer report would have created a reasonable probability of a different result given the totality of the trial evidence, not as adopting a categorical sufficiency-of-the-evidence test. The Fourth Circuit’s approach risks collapsing AEDPA’s demanding threshold into de novo review by treating the state court’s emphasis on evidentiary strength as dispositive error, even though Kyles permits considering the overall evidentiary picture while forbidding only a strict sufficiency test. Because the state court did not clearly contradict Kyles “by its own terms” and could reasonably conclude the report’s impeachment value would not undermine confidence in the verdict, § 2254(d)(1) is not satisfied.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under AEDPA, the question is not whether I would find Brady materiality in the first instance, but whether Maryland’s adjudication was an objectively unreasonable application of this Court’s clearly established Brady/Kyles framework. Kyles clearly establishes that materiality is assessed cumulatively and “is not a sufficiency of evidence test,” so a state court decision that effectively deems suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence immaterial largely because the remaining evidence appears strong misapprehends the governing standard by failing to ask whether disclosure would have produced a reasonable probability of a different result in the trial’s overall evidentiary picture. On these facts—where the suppressed forensic computer report would have substantially impeached a prosecution witness the State treated as central in argument and theory—the Fourth Circuit permissibly concluded that no fairminded jurist could endorse Maryland’s sufficiency-like approach as a reasonable application of Kyles. Given AEDPA’s gatekeeping function, that categorical mismatch between the required cumulative materiality inquiry and the state court’s reasoning is enough to clear § 2254(d)(1)’s bar.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, under AEDPA, the state appellate court unreasonably applied clearly established Supreme Court Brady materiality law (as articulated in Kyles and Strickler) by treating suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence as immaterial based largely on the sufficiency of the remaining evidence rather than evaluating its cumulative effect on the whole case.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1) (AEDPA standard for federal habeas relief) as applied to the Due Process Brady doctrine (U.S. Const. amend. XIV) requiring disclosure of material exculpatory/impeachment evidence; relatedly 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(2) is referenced as an alternative factual-unreasonableness ground.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The state (petitioners: prison superintendent/officials) argues certiorari is warranted because the Fourth Circuit/ federal courts misapplied AEDPA deference and Brady materiality: even if some evidence was suppressed, it was not 'material' because other trial evidence was sufficient to sustain the verdict; the state relies on selective language from Strickler to contend that where remaining evidence supports guilt, nondisclosure does not undermine confidence in the verdict, and therefore the state court's no-materiality determination was at least reasonable (so habeas relief should be barred under Richter's 'fairminded jurists could disagree' standard).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Martin (respondent) argues the petition should be denied because clearly established Supreme Court law (especially Kyles) forbids evaluating Brady materiality as a mere 'sufficiency of the remaining evidence' inquiry; the state appellate court stated Kyles' rule but unreasonably applied it by listing inculpatory evidence without a nuanced, cumulative assessment of how the suppressed evidence would (1) add weight to the defense case and (2) subtract force from the prosecution case, particularly by impeaching a key witness (Carter) whose credibility allegedly anchored the State's theory, jury instructions, and closing argument; Martin further contends Strickler is distinguishable because the suppressed material there would not have meaningfully affected the other evidence, whereas here impeachment would have substantially weakened the prosecution's case.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the best point: Kyles forbids resolving Brady materiality by a bare “still enough to convict” sufficiency test, and a state court cannot evade that rule by reciting the right words while applying the wrong lens. But under Richter our inquiry is whether the state court’s no-materiality result was beyond fairminded disagreement on the state-court record, not whether its explanation was optimally framed; and Strickler permits considering the strength of the remaining proof as part of assessing whether confidence in the verdict is undermined. Here, as Justice Alito and Justice Thomas emphasize, the state court identified the correct reasonable-probability framework and addressed the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory value before concluding the remaining evidence kept confidence in the verdict intact—an application that may be debatable but is not objectively unreasonable under § 2254(d)(1). Accepting respondent’s view would risk converting Kyles into a clearly established requirement of a particular style of cumulative exposition, which AEDPA and Richter do not allow federal courts to impose.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest point: Kyles forbids collapsing Brady materiality into a bare sufficiency-of-the-remaining-evidence test, and reciting the right standard cannot mask use of the wrong lens. But under § 2254(d)(1), as the Chief Justice and Justice Alito emphasize, the question is whether the state court’s no-materiality result was an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established holdings, not whether it performed an ideal, explicitly cumulative exposition; Richter does not permit federal habeas courts to treat arguable analytic shortcuts as per se unreasonableness where the outcome remains debatable among fairminded jurists. Here the state court invoked the correct “reasonable probability” standard and considered the impeachment/exculpatory value in light of the whole record, and given the generality of Brady materiality (as applied through Kyles/Strickler), I cannot say its conclusion is beyond fairminded disagreement. Adopting respondent’s approach would effectively convert Kyles into a clearly established requirement of a particular mode of analysis and invite the kind of federal reweighing of prejudice AEDPA was enacted to forbid.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor are right that Kyles forbids collapsing Brady materiality into a bare “still enough to convict” test, and AEDPA does not require us to credit a state court’s mere incantation of the correct standard if the court in substance applied the wrong one. But reading the state opinion textually—as the Chief Justice stresses—it invoked the “reasonable probability”/confidence-in-the-verdict framework and did address the impeachment/exculpatory force of the suppressed material before weighing it against the other trial proof, which Strickler permits as part of the totality-of-the-evidence inquiry. Under Richter, the question is whether the no-materiality result was beyond fairminded disagreement, and given the generality of the Brady/Kyles materiality standard and the other inculpatory evidence the state court relied upon, I cannot say the state court’s application was objectively unreasonable even if one might reach a different conclusion de novo. The respondents’ approach risks turning Kyles into a clearly established requirement of a particular analytic form rather than a result-focused probability assessment, which AEDPA does not allow on habeas.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s point that Richter does not demand a model opinion and that AEDPA review targets the reasonableness of the result, not the state court’s prose. But the decisive question Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett identify remains: whether the state court meaningfully applied Kyles’ confidence-in-the-verdict framework or instead substituted a sufficiency-style shortcut by treating the remaining evidence as essentially dispositive without grappling with how the suppressed material cumulatively reshapes the credibility contest around Carter and the State’s narrative. AEDPA deference cannot extend to a decision that recites “reasonable probability” while, in substance, applying the wrong constitutional lens—particularly where the withheld evidence strikes at the State’s anchoring witness. On that record, I continue to think the Fourth Circuit could conclude the state court unreasonably applied clearly established Brady law under § 2254(d)(1).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I take the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s point that Richter requires deference to the state court’s result and that remaining evidence strength may figure into a Brady materiality assessment. But Justice Sotomayor (and Justice Barrett) identify the key flaw: Kyles forbids collapsing materiality into a functional sufficiency-of-the-remaining-evidence test, and the state court’s analysis reads in substance like that shortcut—cataloging inculpatory proof as essentially dispositive without a genuine cumulative accounting of how the suppressed evidence would reframe Carter’s credibility and the State’s story. AEDPA deference tolerates reasonable applications of the governing framework; it does not insulate a decision that, while reciting “reasonable probability,” effectively applies a different lens than Kyles requires. Because the misstep is methodological in a way Kyles clearly forecloses—not merely an imperfectly written but substantively faithful application—I would adhere to the Fourth Circuit’s conclusion that § 2254(d)(1) is satisfied.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor rightly stress that Kyles forbids collapsing Brady materiality into a bare “still enough to convict” sufficiency inquiry, and I agree AEDPA deference does not insulate a state court that truly applied the wrong rule. But Richter teaches we do not police opinion-writing and must uphold a merits determination so long as the result falls within the range fairminded jurists could reach under the governing holdings; here the state court recited the correct “reasonable probability/undermines confidence” standard and addressed the suppressed impeachment value in light of the trial record. Even if its discussion leaned heavily on other inculpatory proof, Strickler permits considering the remaining evidence as part of the materiality calculus, and I cannot say the no-materiality result is beyond fairminded disagreement under § 2254(d)(1). For that reason, I remain persuaded AEDPA bars relief on this record.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest opposing point: Kyles forbids collapsing Brady materiality into a bare “still enough to convict” sufficiency test, especially where the suppressed evidence impeaches an anchoring witness like Carter. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, AEDPA and Richter require us to assess the reasonableness of the state court’s result, not to demand a particular style of expressly cumulative exposition, and the state court here did cite the correct “reasonable probability/confidence in the verdict” standard and did address the impeachment value before considering the rest of the trial record. Even if the opinion leans heavily on other inculpatory proof, that does not necessarily show it applied the wrong constitutional lens in substance; under Strickler, remaining-evidence strength is part of the confidence-in-the-verdict inquiry, and fairminded jurists could agree with the state court’s no-materiality conclusion on this record. Given § 2254(d)(1)’s constraints, I do not think the Fourth Circuit’s contrary view is compelled beyond fairminded disagreement.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh make the strongest point that Richter requires deference to the state court’s result and does not impose an opinion-writing requirement, and I agree we cannot demand a Kyles-style cumulative exposition as such. But Kyles clearly establishes that materiality is not a “still enough to convict” sufficiency inquiry, and Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor persuasively show the state court’s reasoning functionally collapsed into that shortcut—cataloging other inculpatory proof without a whole-case reassessment of how the suppressed evidence would cumulatively undermine Carter and the State’s narrative. Under AEDPA we defer to reasonable applications of governing law, not to a decision that recites the correct words while substantively applying the wrong lens, and this makes the case ill-suited for summary reversal. Given the centrality of the anchoring witness, I cannot say fairminded disagreement extends to a sufficiency-style rationale masquerading as Kyles materiality.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s Richter point is the strongest for petitioner: AEDPA asks about the reasonableness of the result, and a state court may consider the strength of the remaining evidence in the Brady materiality calculus. But that principle does not answer Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s core objection that Kyles clearly establishes a distinct, whole-case “confidence in the verdict” framework—one that is not satisfied by a functional “still enough to convict” sufficiency shortcut, especially when the suppressed evidence impeaches the prosecution’s anchoring witness and narrative. Where the state court’s analysis, in substance, treats the rest of the record as dispositive without grappling with how the withheld evidence both adds to the defense and subtracts from the State’s theory, Richter deference cannot convert an application of the wrong lens into a reasonable one. I therefore continue to think the Fourth Circuit could conclude § 2254(d)(1) is satisfied, and this is not a proper vehicle to insulate that kind of verdict-reliability error from federal review absent clearer congressional direction.

John Roberts.reasoning: Because the Brady claim was adjudicated on the merits in state court, AEDPA § 2254(d)(1) permits relief only if that court’s application of clearly established law was not merely wrong but objectively unreasonable under Richter’s fairminded-jurist standard, on the record before the state court. Although Kyles states that materiality is not a sufficiency-of-the-evidence test, the state appellate court’s discussion of the remaining inculpatory proof can still be a permissible way to assess whether the suppressed computer report creates a “reasonable probability” of a different result, and Strickler likewise contemplates considering the strength of the prosecution case in that inquiry. On this record, where the state court identified the correct Brady standard and concluded that other evidence independently supported guilt, I cannot say its no-materiality determination was beyond the bounds of reasonable disagreement, so federal habeas relief is barred by § 2254(d).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under § 2254(d)(1), the only relevant question is whether the state appellate court’s no-materiality determination was an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court holdings, not whether a federal court would have performed a more “nuanced” written analysis. Kyles and Strickler clearly establish that materiality is not a mere sufficiency-of-the-remaining-evidence test and requires consideration of the suppressed evidence in the context of the whole case, but they do not clearly establish any particular format of explanation a state court must provide, and Richter requires us to uphold the state result so long as fairminded jurists could disagree. Given the state court’s acknowledgment of the governing standard and its conclusion that the remaining proof supported confidence in the verdict even accounting for the impeachment/exculpatory material, the Fourth Circuit’s contrary approach risks impermissibly extending Brady/Kyles into a freestanding requirement of granular cumulative exposition. On this record, the petitioner has not shown an error “beyond any possibility for fairminded disagreement,” so AEDPA bars relief.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under AEDPA, the question is not whether the federal court believes the suppressed computer report was material under Brady, but whether the state appellate court’s no-materiality determination was so wrong that no fairminded jurist could agree. Reading the state opinion straightforwardly, it identified the correct “reasonable probability” standard and then assessed the effect of the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory material in light of the other trial proof, concluding that the remaining evidence of guilt was substantial enough that confidence in the verdict was not undermined. Although Kyles forbids reducing materiality to a bare sufficiency test, a state court does not unreasonably apply Kyles merely by emphasizing the strength of the State’s case when, as here, it considered the purported impeachment value and still found it insufficient to create a reasonable probability of a different result. The Fourth Circuit’s contrary approach effectively substitutes its own reweighing of the cumulative record for the state court’s prejudice/materiality judgment, which § 2254(d)(1) does not permit.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The state appellate court recited Kyles/Strickler but did not do the work those cases require: it treated materiality largely as a sufficiency-of-the-remaining-evidence inquiry, listing other inculpatory proof rather than assessing, in light of the trial record, the cumulative effect of the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory material on “the whole case.” That reasoning functions as the kind of shortcut Kyles forbids—finding nondisclosure immaterial because the rest of the evidence could still sustain a verdict—especially where the suppressed material went to impeaching Carter, a witness the State anchored in its theory and argument, and thus could both add weight to the defense and subtract force from the prosecution. Under AEDPA, deference does not extend to a decision that quotes the correct standard but unreasonably applies it by failing to engage with all the circumstances and the combined impact of the suppressed evidence on the verdict’s reliability. Accordingly, the Fourth Circuit’s refusal to accept that unreasonable application does not warrant reversal, and habeas relief is not barred on the State’s view of Richter’s “fairminded jurists could disagree” gloss when the state court’s analysis conflicts with Kyles’ governing framework.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under § 2254(d)(1), the question is not whether I would find Brady materiality in the first instance, but whether the state appellate court unreasonably applied clearly established law—principally Kyles and Strickler—governing the “reasonable probability” inquiry. Kyles makes plain that materiality is “not a sufficiency of evidence test” and requires assessing the cumulative effect of all suppressed evidence on the whole case, including how it would both impeach the State’s proof and bolster the defense; here, the state court largely cataloged the remaining inculpatory evidence and treated that as dispositive, without a genuine cumulative accounting of how the suppressed forensic/impeachment material would have undercut the prosecution’s key witness (Carter) who anchored the State’s narrative at trial. Given the centrality of that witness to the State’s theory and argument, fairminded jurists could not defend a materiality analysis that effectively collapses into “the evidence was still enough to convict,” which is the very approach Kyles forbids. AEDPA deference is substantial, but it does not permit a state court to recite the right standard and then apply a different one in substance—so habeas relief is not barred on this record.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Because the state appellate court adjudicated the Brady claim on the merits, AEDPA supplies the rule of decision and § 2254(d)(1) bars relief unless the decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court holdings. Kyles and Strickler clearly establish that Brady materiality is not a bare sufficiency-of-the-remaining-evidence test and requires considering the cumulative effect of suppressed evidence on the whole case, including impeachment of key witnesses—but AEDPA asks a different question: whether every fairminded jurist would have to say the state court’s application was beyond the bounds of reasonable disagreement at the time. Given that the state court recited the correct Kyles/Strickler standard and then emphasized the strength of other inculpatory evidence in concluding no reasonable probability of a different result, I cannot say its materiality determination was one no fairminded jurist could reach; at most it reflects a debatable application of a general standard, which AEDPA forbids us to correct. Even if the Fourth Circuit thought the state court’s analysis resembled a sufficiency review, Richter’s deference means federal habeas relief is unavailable unless the misapplication is unmistakable under the controlling holdings, and this record leaves room for reasonable disagreement about whether the suppressed impeachment would have altered the verdict given the remaining evidence.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The specific constitutional right is Brady due process, and the decisive element here is materiality—whether, in light of the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory material, there is a reasonable probability of a different result when the evidence is considered cumulatively under Kyles. But on federal habeas the question is narrower: under AEDPA and Richter, whether the state court’s no-materiality decision was so obviously contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Brady/Kyles law that no fairminded jurist could agree. Even assuming the state appellate court’s written discussion leaned heavily on the strength of the remaining evidence, Richter instructs that we review the reasonableness of the decision itself, not demand a more “nuanced” or transparently holistic explanation; and Strickler confirms that where the record still contains substantial inculpatory proof, a state court may reasonably conclude nondisclosure does not undermine confidence in the verdict. Given that posture and the presence of other inculpatory evidence beyond Carter, I would hold that § 2254(d)(1) bars relief because the state court’s materiality determination was at least within the range of fairminded disagreement.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: AEDPA bars relief unless the state court’s adjudication was not just wrong but an unreasonable application of clearly established Brady materiality law, and Kyles clearly establishes that materiality is “not a sufficiency of evidence test” but a cumulative, whole-case assessment of whether disclosure would undermine confidence in the verdict. On this record, the state appellate court’s analysis appears to have treated the suppressed computer/forensic impeachment as immaterial largely because other evidence could still support guilt, without grappling with how impeaching the prosecution’s key witness (Carter) could both subtract force from the State’s theory and add weight to the defense cumulatively—precisely the mode of reasoning Kyles forbids. Even under Richter’s fairminded-jurist deference, applying a sufficiency-style rationale in lieu of Kyles’ cumulative reasonable-probability inquiry crosses from debatable weighing into misapplication of the governing rule. Consistent with restraint, the proper disposition is to uphold the grant of relief (or at minimum deny summary reversal), because the state court’s materiality reasoning rests on the wrong lens rather than a permissible, deferential application of Kyles/Strickler to the whole trial record.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under § 2254(d)(1), the question is not whether the suppressed computer/forensic report and related impeachment would have compelled acquittal, but whether the state appellate court’s no-materiality determination was a reasonable application of clearly established Brady materiality law. Kyles makes clear that materiality “is not a sufficiency of evidence test” and requires a cumulative, whole-case assessment of how suppressed evidence both adds force to the defense and subtracts force from the prosecution; here, the state court’s analysis largely tallied the remaining inculpatory proof and treated that sufficiency as dispositive, without grappling with how impeaching the prosecution’s key witness (Carter) could have altered the trial’s narrative, closing arguments, and the jury’s credibility choices. Given that this suppressed evidence went to the reliability of the State’s central theory rather than a collateral point, the Fourth Circuit could reasonably conclude that the state court’s approach departed from Kyles/Strickler’s reasonable-probability framework in a way that no fairminded jurist could endorse as a faithful application, even under Richter’s demanding deference. AEDPA’s constraints are real, but Congress did not authorize state courts to replace Brady’s cumulative materiality inquiry with a sufficiency-of-the-remaining-evidence shortcut that functionally forecloses review of serious nondisclosure affecting the fairness of the trial.
